record.title: CogGym reports a large matched human–model evaluation suite with persistent behavioral gaps
record.summary: A September 18 preprint introduces CogGym, a human-in-the-loop pipeline that standardizes cognitive-science experiments into a common format for matched human and language-model evaluation. The initial release reports 258 experiments from 100 papers across text, image and video, with 50 language models evaluated. On the paper’s reported human–model fit measure, the best models reach R² of 0.59 for text, 0.58 for image and 0.43 for video, below estimated human split-half references of 0.93, 0.95 and 0.92. A 15-experiment replication with 521 participants reports closer agreement between new and original human responses than between Gemini 3.1 Pro and the original responses. These are author-reported results; the 15-study check is a subset, not an independent reproduction of the full suite.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report standardizing 258 cognitive experiments from 100 papers and evaluating 50 language models on matched human-response tasks spanning text, image and video.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports best model–human fit R² values of 0.59 for text, 0.58 for image and 0.43 for video, below human split-half references of 0.93, 0.95 and 0.92; these estimates use reliability-eligible/recoverable subsets rather than all 258 experiments.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For a 15-experiment replication subset with 521 participants, the authors report that new human responses agreed more closely with original human responses (mean R² 0.84) than Gemini 3.1 Pro responses did (mean R² 0.62). This subset check does not validate the full suite.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The preprint does not establish that model–human fit is equivalent to general intelligence, transfers beyond its selected commonsense experiments or model set, or causally improves with model scale.

evidence_gaps.description: The framework, corpus conversion and model scores have not been independently audited or reproduced by the research desk.

The main release focuses on commonsense tasks, and human split-half references rely on 172 recoverable exports; some analyses cover smaller eligibility subsets. Coverage outside these tasks and modalities is unknown.
Cross-sectional associations between model size/release date and human-response fit do not establish causal scaling effects or broad behavioral equivalence.

brief.importance_rationale: If the framework and measurements hold up, a shared pipeline spanning 258 cognitive experiments and three modalities could improve evaluation coverage and expose behavioral limits missed by formal benchmarks. Score 5 reflects useful field-wide infrastructure, not truth confidence; the dataset is scoped to commonsense experiments and the reported comparisons remain author-run.
limitations: All results are author-reported in one preprint; the research desk did not run the code/data or reproduce the comparisons.
The initial suite focuses on human commonsense reasoning; it does not measure general intelligence or establish that models think like humans.

The 258-experiment inventory is not the analysis denominator for every metric: human reliability references use 172 recoverable archived exports, while the model reliability subset has 179 experiments.
A 15-experiment replication with 521 participants is a bounded validity check and does not independently reproduce the full 258-experiment model evaluation.
Associations with model size and release date do not establish causal effects of scaling; model lineups and task coverage are heterogeneous.
brief.summary: A September 18 preprint introduces CogGym, a human-in-the-loop pipeline that standardizes cognitive-science experiments into a common format for matched human and language-model evaluation. The initial release reports 258 experiments from 100 papers across text, image and video, with 50 language models evaluated. On the paper’s reported human–model fit measure, the best models reach R² of 0.59 for text, 0.58 for image and 0.43 for video, below estimated human split-half references of 0.93, 0.95 and 0.92. A 15-experiment replication with 521 participants reports closer agreement between new and original human responses than between Gemini 3.1 Pro and the original responses. These are author-reported results; the 15-study check is a subset, not an independent reproduction of the full suite.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 258 standardized experiments from 100 papers and 50 evaluated models. Best reported model–human R² is 0.59 (text), 0.58 (image) and 0.43 (video), compared with human split-half references 0.93, 0.95 and 0.92. In a 15-experiment, 521-participant replication check, new human responses have mean R² 0.84 against original responses versus 0.62 for Gemini 3.1 Pro.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper does not report a comparable inference-cost or human-study cost analysis for the full 50-model suite. The 521-participant replication is limited to 15 sampled experiments.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint documents the framework, experiment corpus, evaluation measures and author-reported analyses. the research desk did not download or run the code/data, reproduce any study, or independently validate model or human scores.
technical.mechanism: A semi-automated pipeline with researcher review converts heterogeneous cognitive-science experiments into an Experiment Markup Language (EML) representation of instructions, stimuli, trial structure and response format. The standardized tasks can then be rendered for humans and models and their response patterns compared.
technical.regime: Initial suite: 258 cognitive experiments from 100 papers, focused on commonsense reasoning, with text, image and video stimuli; 50 frontier/open-weight models. Human split-half estimates use response items with at least 10 observations and 172 recoverable archived exports (80 text, 33 image, 59 video); the reliability-eligible model subset has 179 experiments. A separate random 15-experiment replication recruited 521 Prolific participants and evaluated Gemini 3.1 Pro against original data.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes an EML format and human-in-the-loop conversion workflow, but the research desk did not inspect or execute the released code/data. The authors’ 15-experiment human replication is an internal validity check, not an independent replication of the full model comparison.
technical.strongest_baseline: Human split-half reliability, estimated from random participant splits and corrected with Spearman–Brown, is the paper’s human agreement reference: R² 0.93 for text, 0.95 for image and 0.92 for video. In the 15-experiment replication subset, newly collected human responses (mean R² 0.84) are compared with Gemini 3.1 Pro (0.62) against original human data.

brief.title: CogGym reports a large matched human–model evaluation suite with persistent behavioral gaps
brief.why_it_matters: A reusable, multimodal translation layer for cognitive-science experiments could make human–model behavioral comparisons easier to update as models change. The reported results also caution against treating strong math or coding performance as evidence of human-like judgments. The current release focuses on commonsense tasks, has missing or unrecoverable archived data in some analyses, and does not establish broad cognitive equivalence or a causal effect of scale.
